<reason>PRO kept the debate anchored to the motion as written: the stipulated set is jobs where the degree doesn't drive performance, and the employer is the decider (the antibiotics analogy neatly defused CON's "who decides / changes nothing" trap). PRO also exploited CON's own "barely changed" admission and forced CON to retreat from a performance-prediction case to a pile-sorting-convenience case, then weighed asymmetric costs (a few more résumés vs. millions locked out). CON's strongest material was original and clever — a posted degree requirement is a transparent, connectionless, earnable rule, and reading capacity is fixed — but it leaned on shaky premises (that "degree or equivalent" is nearly universal, so PRO's floor is the status quo) and its closing treated PRO's explicitly posted multi-route floor as if it were an opaque vacuum, which mischaracterizes the live proposal. PRO's "adding doors doesn't shrink the building / removes a requirement, not a credential" answered the vacuum image adequately, while CON never fully rebutted the point that the floor is itself a visible rule. CON's second rebuttal was also clipped. Competitive but PRO gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A2/[A4.5] turn: answering the "4000 résumés" question with a broadened posted floor, then observing that CON had stopped defending the degree as a performance predictor and was now defending it as a convenient pile-cutter — "that is my case" — followed by the who-bears-the-cost weighing. CON's [B4.3] transparency counter (a visible rule became an opaque one) was the sharpest reply, but it depended on the contested claim that PRO's floor is merely the status quo.</best_rebuttal>
